opus-5.5.text:
It's a really interesting dynamic, and it cuts both ways.

On one hand, a large technology company brings a certain baseline of trust. Doctors and hospital administrators assume there's serious infrastructure behind the product: security teams, compliance processes, legal review, and the resources to support a deployment over many years. When you're talking about patient data and clinical workflows, that matters a lot. A hospital doesn't want to integrate something into its EHR and then find out eighteen months later that the vendor ran out of runway. So big companies often get a hearing that a small startup might struggle to get.

But there's also skepticism toward big tech specifically. Many clinicians worry about what happens to the data, whether they're being used to build a product that will eventually be sold back to them, or whether the company really understands medicine or just sees healthcare as another market to enter. There's a history of technology arriving in medicine with big promises and adding clerical burden instead. Electronic health records are the classic example. So when a large tech company shows up, some doctors are already bracing for that.

Startups have almost the opposite profile. They're often founded by, or work very closely with, practicing clinicians, so they can be very specific about a pain point. "We'll take thirty minutes of documentation off your evening" is concrete and believable. Doctors can relate to that. The concern is durability, validation, and whether the startup has done rigorous evaluation or is moving fast and hoping nothing breaks in a clinical setting.

What I've seen is that, in the end, the brand matters less than two things. First, does the tool solve a problem the clinician actually feels every day? Second, is there credible evidence that it's safe and accurate, ideally peer-reviewed and tested on populations like their own patients? If you can show both, doctors are quite pragmatic. If you can't, a big logo won't save you, and a scrappy startup story won't either.

There's also a middle path that's becoming common: partnerships. A startup builds the clinically focused product, a larger company provides the infrastructure or the model, and a health system serves as the clinical partner that validates it. That combination tends to address the trust concerns on all sides. Healthcare is fundamentally a trust business, and whoever earns that trust through transparency and evidence, regardless of size, is the one that gets adopted.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts clinicians’ skepticism and data concerns about large tech companies with startups’ clinician-focused appeal, suggesting some doctors may feel more wary or threatened by big-tech healthcare AI.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I've thought about a lot, because the perception gap is real and it cuts both ways.

When a big company like Google or Microsoft shows up with a healthcare AI product, doctors tend to have two reactions at once. On one hand, there's a baseline level of trust in the engineering. They assume the infrastructure is solid, the security is handled, the thing won't fall over. On the other hand, there's a lot of skepticism about motives and staying power. Physicians have watched big tech enter and exit healthcare several times. Google Health shut down, Microsoft HealthVault shut down, Amazon Care shut down. So the question I hear is, "Will this still exist in three years, and what happens to my workflow and my data if it doesn't?" And then there's the deeper concern about what the company actually wants. Is this about helping me take care of patients, or is it about getting access to clinical data to train the next model?

Startups get almost the mirror image. Doctors often find them more responsive and more willing to actually sit in the clinic and understand the workflow. A founder will show up, watch a physician chart for a day, and change the product the next week. That builds a lot of goodwill. But the skepticism there is about durability and seriousness. Is this company going to survive? Do they understand regulation? Do they understand liability? A physician is putting their license behind whatever the tool recommends, so "move fast and break things" is exactly the wrong message in that room.

What I've seen work is when either kind of company earns credibility through the same mechanisms. The product has to show up inside the systems doctors already use, rather than asking them to open another window. It needs clinical evidence that looks like clinical evidence, meaning prospective studies, not just a retrospective benchmark number. And it needs clinical champions, because doctors trust other doctors far more than they trust any company. The most effective adoption I've witnessed usually came from a respected physician in the department saying, "I've used this for six months and it saves me forty minutes a day," not from a vendor pitch.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say perception of the company sets the starting point for trust, but it doesn't determine the outcome. Big tech starts with trust in competence and a deficit in intent. Startups start with trust in intent and a deficit in competence and longevity. Both have to close their gap, and the way you close it is by being boring in the right ways: reliable, transparent about what the model does and doesn't do, and clearly accountable when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says doctors may distrust large tech companies’ motives and worry about access to clinical data, but it does not clearly say they feel more threatened by those companies’ healthcare AI than by startups.

astra-6.text:
I think trust plays a big role, but it’s not as simple as doctors trusting a large company more than a startup. A large technology company might have a reputation for strong engineering and the resources to support a product over time. At the same time, doctors may have questions about how patient data will be used and how committed that company is to healthcare.

A startup can build trust by being very focused on a particular clinical problem and working closely with doctors. If you listen to their feedback and make something that fits into their workflow, that can matter more than the name of the company. But you still have to demonstrate that the product is reliable and that you’ll be around to support it.

Ultimately, I think the company’s reputation gets you an initial conversation. Adoption depends on whether doctors see evidence that the tool helps their patients or saves them time, and whether they understand its limitations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trust, company reputation, and adoption, but does not say that doctors may feel more threatened by AI from a large technology company than by AI from a startup.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a tradeoff. A large technology company has a recognizable name, and that can give doctors confidence that it has the resources to build something reliable and support it over time. But that same company may raise questions about patient privacy: What happens to the data, and what does the company ultimately want to do with it?

A startup can feel more focused on a particular clinical problem and more willing to work closely with doctors. But then the questions are: Has this actually been validated? Will the company still be around in a few years? Can we trust it with something that matters to patient care?

So the company’s reputation can influence whether a doctor is willing to try the product. For sustained adoption, though, I think you have to demonstrate that it works for their patients, fits into their workflow, and has clear limitations. That trust has to be earned regardless of the size of the company.

r001.rationale: The response says large technology companies may raise patient-privacy concerns, but it does not suggest doctors feel more threatened by their AI than by startup AI; it presents distinct concerns about both.
